findings.title: Downloaded libduckdb.dylib is dlopen'd + JIT-linked with no checksum/signature verification (TLS is the only integrity control)
findings.description: _download_libduckdb() (utils.py:50-91) builds the release URL purely from duckdb.__version__ -- https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/releases/download/v{version}/libduckdb-osx-universal.zip (utils.py:51-56) -- then `with urlopen(url) as resp: data = resp.read()` (utils.py:83-84), opens it in memory as `zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(data))` (utils.py:85), extracts the single hardcoded member `libduckdb.dylib` to ~/.numbduck/lib/<version>/libduckdb.dylib (utils.py:88-89), and the caller does `return load_lib_path(downloaded)` (utils.py:130), which is numbox's `CDLL(path, mode=RTLD_GLOBAL)` (numbox/core/bindings/utils.py:178-180). Loading RTLD_GLOBAL is exactly the mechanism by which the dylib's `duckdb_*` symbols become resolvable to llvmlite's JIT linker for every @cres binding (loader.md sec.5), so the downloaded bytes are not merely opened -- their native code is executed in-process under the user's identity. There is NO integrity check anywhere in the file (confirmed: no hashlib/sha256/codesign/hmac/ssl-pinning in utils.py): no pinned SHA-256 compared against the bytes, no GPG/minisign signature, no macOS codesign --verify, no size sanity. The DEFAULT urlopen SSL context does validate the GitHub host certificate (PEP 476), so a passive on-path MITM cannot substitute the zip without a trusted-CA/trust-store compromise -- but TLS is then the ONLY line of defense. It provides zero protection against the two material supply-chain vectors: (a) a compromised/replaced GitHub release asset (a pinned per-version digest in numbduck would DETECT this; TLS would not), and (b) any redirect off HTTPS (urlopen follows 30x). The consent surfaces actively weaken this: NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 (utils.py:57-58) silently authorizes the unverified download with no prompt (the CI/non-interactive path), and the interactive input() prompt (utils.py:67) tells the user it will 'download the standalone libduckdb.dylib and cache it' but does NOT disclose that the download is unverified, so an informed-consent 'y' is not actually informed.
findings.impact: If the downloaded bytes are ever altered before load (compromised upstream release asset, CA/trust-store compromise enabling TLS interception, or an off-HTTPS redirect), the substituted dylib is dlopen'd RTLD_GLOBAL and its symbols JIT-linked into every binding = arbitrary native code execution in the host process under the user. Likelihood is bounded by mitigating factors: macOS-only path, only reached when the installed wheel is C-API-stripped (duckdb-python >=1.4.1), and gated behind consent (NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 or interactive 'y'); TLS protects the common transport case. Hence medium, not high.
findings.recommendation: Pin and verify before extracting/loading: ship a per-duckdb-version SHA-256 (ideally the digest published in the upstream DuckDB release notes / a signed manifest), compute hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() on the downloaded bytes, and refuse to extract or load on mismatch. Where feasible add macOS codesign --verify on the extracted dylib for defense-in-depth. Make the interactive prompt state explicitly that the artifact is verified against a pinned digest (or, if not, that it is unverified) so consent is informed; do not let NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 bypass the digest check. See sibling finding DCK-wrap-SEC-1 which flags the same root issue from the ducklib import side; this unit owns the loader-side fix.

findings.title: Version-keyed cache dylib is reloaded and executed on every run with no re-verification, turning a one-time tamper into persistent code execution
findings.description: _find_standalone_libduckdb() (utils.py:33-47) returns the cached path ~/.numbduck/lib/<version>/libduckdb.dylib whenever the file merely EXISTS (utils.py:41-43, `if os.path.isfile(cached): return cached`), and load_duckdb() then dlopens it RTLD_GLOBAL (utils.py:121). No digest or signature is recomputed on the cache hit -- the existence check is the only gate. The cache directory is created with `os.makedirs(_LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_DIR, exist_ok=True)` (utils.py:86) using the default umask (no explicit mode=0o700), and the file is written directly to its final path (utils.py:88-89), not via temp+atomic-rename. Consequences: (1) Even if UTL-SEC-1's download were verified, any later local write to that cache file (by any process running as the same user) is loaded as native code indefinitely, never re-checked -- a one-shot compromise becomes permanent. (2) The non-atomic write means a crash mid-write, or a concurrent loader, can dlopen a truncated/partial binary. The same 'exists -> load unverified' pattern also applies to the Homebrew search paths /opt/homebrew/lib and /usr/local/lib (utils.py:23-26, 44-46); on Intel-Homebrew layouts /usr/local is user-owned, so that is an additional unverified standalone source, though loading an admin-installed system dylib from a standard prefix is conventional and is the user/OS's responsibility.
findings.impact: A single successful tamper of ~/.numbduck/lib/<ver>/libduckdb.dylib (or a poisoned-at-download file from UTL-SEC-1) persists across all future numbduck imports with no detection, yielding durable arbitrary-code-execution in the user's processes. Scope is local (default makedirs perms ~0755 prevent OTHER local users from writing, so the attacker must already run as the same user); the value is persistence and widening UTL-SEC-1's window, hence low.
findings.recommendation: Re-verify the pinned SHA-256 on every cache hit in _find_standalone_libduckdb(), not only at download time, and refuse/re-download on mismatch. Create the cache dir with mode=0o700 and write via a temp file + os.replace for atomicity. Optionally codesign --verify cached/standalone dylibs before load.

notes:
Scope: SEC audit of /home/erik/projects/numbduck/numbduck/utils.py (the DuckDB shared-library loader); load mechanism cross-checked against numbox load_lib_path (/home/erik/projects/numbox/numbox/core/bindings/utils.py:167-183, CDLL RTLD_GLOBAL) and understanding/loader.md. Two findings; the focus's other enumerated items were assessed and judged NOT to be defects:

- os.remove of a user-influenced path (utils.py:38-40): the removed path old_cached = ~/.numbduck/lib/libduckdb.dylib is fully derived from module constants + os.path.expanduser('~'); it carries NO attacker-controllable component except $HOME, and an attacker who controls process env already wins via DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES/PYTHONPATH. os.remove on a symlink unlinks the link, not its target, so it is not an arbitrary-delete primitive. The unguarded call can raise OSError on a permission/race error -- a robustness gap, not a security defect.

- NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB env trust (utils.py:34-36): loads an arbitrary user-specified path as native code RTLD_GLOBAL. This is the documented override; controlling a target's process environment is already full compromise (LD_PRELOAD/DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES equivalents). Accepted-by-design, not a vuln. NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 (utils.py:57) is a convenience consent flag, not a separate vuln -- its security relevance (silently authorizing an UNVERIFIED download) is folded into UTL-SEC-1's recommendation.

- Zip member extraction (utils.py:85,88-89): the member name is the hardcoded literal 'libduckdb.dylib' and the destination is a fixed path; the archive's own entry names are never used to build a filesystem path, so there is NO zip-slip / path-traversal. A decompression-bomb (tiny zip, huge member) could OOM, but delivering a malicious zip already requires the release/transport compromise of UTL-SEC-1, where shipping a malicious dylib directly is simpler; subsumed, not separately material.

- Interactive input() gate (utils.py:67): functions as a consent control (a mitigation for UTL-SEC-1), not an attack surface. In non-interactive contexts without NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 it raises EOFError (robustness). Its only security-relevant weakness -- it does not disclose that the download is unverified -- is captured in UTL-SEC-1.

- duckdb.__version__ is interpolated unsanitized into both the download URL (utils.py:51) and the cache filesystem path (utils.py:20 makedirs at :86); a value containing '/' or '..' could traverse. But the value is trusted dependency metadata (PEP 440 strings have no slashes); an attacker able to set it has already installed a malicious duckdb. Not a real defect.

The @cres FFI wrappers and length/pointer-across-the-C-boundary surface are owned by DCK-wrap-SEC (concluded SOUND). UTL-SEC-1 is the loader-side owner of the supply-chain issue that DCK-wrap-SEC-1 raised from the import side; both are medium/high-confidence and consistent.
